P003|The AI Scientist: Towards Fully Automated Open-Ended Scientific Discovery|https://arxiv.org/abs/2408.06292|2024-08|arXiv preprint|0|Automated ML research|End-to-end ML research from a code template: idea generation, experiments, paper write-up and LLM review, on three templates (2D diffusion, NanoGPT language modeling, grokking on modular arithmetic) with four LLMs (Claude Sonnet 3.5, GPT-4o, DeepSeek Coder, Llama-3.1 405b)|closed loop; accumulation|External artifacts only: research ideas, experiment code edited from the template, and papers; the LLM pipeline itself does not change|R0|Section 3: ideas are grown in an archive "using LLMs as the mutation operator" and Aider "implements plan-directed code-level changes to the experiment template"; nothing in the pipeline (prompts, scaffold, model) is changed by the system. The GPT-4o reviewer is described as feeding the archive, but Section 6 says ideas were generated "without waiting for paper evaluations to be appended to the archive", so in the reported experiments the reviewer is only a final evaluation and is not counted as a feedback source. Cost: Section 3 says the template's baseline run "completes within a few minutes"; the experiment timeout is 7200 seconds (Appendix B); a run of about 50 ideas takes about 12 hours on 8 H100s (Section 6). P004|Gödel Agent: A Self-Referential Agent Framework for Recursively Self-Improvement|https://arxiv.org/abs/2410.04444|2024-10|arXiv preprint|0;2|Agent self-improvement; Mathematics|DROP reading comprehension; MGSM multilingual math; MMLU multi-task; GPQA science QA; case study on Game of 24|closed loop; self-reference; accumulation|The agent's own running code, changed by monkey patching: the task policy (solver) and, in the case study, the self-improvement logic itself|R4 (changes to the improvement logic shown only qualitatively, in the Game of 24 case study)|Section 3: a Gödel Agent "updates both the policy π and the meta-learning algorithm I recursively"; Section 6.3 (Game of 24): it "enhances its optimization process by not only retrieving error messages but also using the error-trace library for more detailed analysis. The code listings in Appendices C and E show only improved solver policies, not a modified improvement module|automated evaluation|fully automatic|multi-generation single lineage|6 independent self-improvement cycles per task with at most 30 iterations each (Section 5.2); 100 optimization trials on MGSM for the robustness analysis (Section 6.2)|not reported|fully reversible|RSI|in-task|With GPT-3.5 at test time (Gödel-base), test scores beat Meta Agent Search on all four benchmarks: DROP F1 80.9 vs 79.4, MGSM 64.2% vs 53.4%, MMLU 70.9% vs 69.6%, GPQA 34.9% vs 34.6% (Table 1); on Game of 24 one run rewrote its solver into a search algorithm and reached 100% (Section 6.3)|In 100 MGSM trials it made erroneous changes: 4% terminated unexpectedly, typically after modifying its own recursive improvement module, 92% had temporary performance drops, and 14% ended worse than the initial policy (Section 6.2); the unconstrained version's large gains come mainly from spontaneously calling stronger models such as GPT-4o (Section 5.3); from weaker initial policies it did not surpass Tree of Thought on Game of 24, and with stronger initial policies it reached its limit "without further enhancing its optimization capabilities" (Section 6.3); not compared with complex engineered agent systems, and the experiments only demonstrate feasibility (Limitations); the system may become too complex to understand and improve itself (Limitations); cost grows with its growing historical memory (Appendix D)|full text|medium|Feedback details: the agent's interact or evaluate action scores the current solver on a validation set (Section 4.1: "a validation set can be used to provide feedback"; Algorithm 1, U(E, π)); the LLM then decides whether to keep a change, try another, or revert (Section 6.2: it can "revert to a previous optimal algorithm when performance declines"). The modifying model is GPT-4o and the solver is tested with GPT-3.5 (Appendix B). Loop: people write the goal prompt, the initial policy (CoT) and the environment interface; no person takes part during a cycle. Evidence: each task is optimized on its own validation set and tested on that benchmark's test set; no transfer to other tasks or models is reported, although the abstract claims generalizability. The best agent so far is also the meta-agent that makes the next change, so the edited code takes part in later improvement steps|R2|Section 1: SICA “eliminates the distinction between meta-agent and target agent, and is capable of editing its own codebase to improve itself”; Section 3: “SICA takes the best performing agent from the archive up until this point as the meta-agent, which is instructed to look through the archive, identify an improvement, and implement it” (Algorithm 1). The changes reported in Appendix D are new tools and routing (smart editor, diff-based editing, code context summarizer, AST and hybrid symbol locators, file edit routing in MainAgent); none of them is reported to change the meta-improvement procedure (archive explorer, meta-improvement prompt) or the outer loop, whose utility function (Equations 1-2) and selection rule are fixed|automated evaluation|fully automatic|open-ended population or archive|15 iterations in the main run (Table 1, iterations 0-15); 9 iterations in the AIME and GPQA run (Figure 4)|not reported|fully reversible|self-improvement|in-task|From iteration 0 to 15 on the same benchmarks used for selection: SWE-Bench Verified subset 17% to 51% (peak 53% at iteration 14), LiveCodeBench 65% to 71%, file editing 82% to 91%, symbol location 35% to 40%, with average time per problem 130 s to 115 s and cost USD 1.91 to 1.70 (Table 1); on AIME 2024 and GPQA Diamond the gains were marginal (Figure 4)|Little improvement on AIME and GPQA, where the agent system as a whole averaged 76% while o3-mini alone scores 87% and 79%; the main agent often just delegated to the o3-mini reasoning sub-agent, and the added reasoning components may interrupt the reasoning model's chain of thought (Section 4, Figure 4); it was hard for the agent to come up with truly novel and feasible modification ideas, and a bad idea costs a long editing step plus an even more expensive benchmark run (Limitations); early feature ideas heavily shaped later ones, so poor initial ideas (e.g. fixating on caching open files) lowered later ones, which may make runs high-variance (Limitations); the short 5-minute timeout and per-problem cost cap lower the initial scores, and much of the initial improvement comes from faster file editing and lower cost rather than from what SWE-Bench normally measures (Limitations); the low symbol-location scores are attributed to poor benchmark data quality (Section 4, footnote 3); improvement from scaffolding alone appears limited (Safety Considerations)|full text|medium|Feedback details: each new agent is run on the benchmark set and scored by a fixed utility U = 0.5 x normalised score + 0.25 x cost term (capped at USD 10 per problem) + 0.25 x time term (300 s timeout), halved on timeout (Section 3, Equations 1-2); the agent with the highest utility in the archive becomes the next meta-agent and the base for the next iteration, and every agent with its results stays in the archive (Section 3, Algorithm 1). File editing is scored by closeness to the target file, symbol location by the returned location, SWE-Bench and LiveCodeBench by their own tests (Section 4). An asynchronous LLM overseer, called every 30 s, can notify or cancel running agents to stop loops and off-task behaviour (Section 3.1, Appendix A.2); it does not decide which agent is kept. The meta-improvement step itself uses an archive explorer sub-agent and LLM reasoning sub-agents to pick a change (Appendix B). Models: Sonnet 3.5 (v2) for most agents and o3-mini for the reasoning sub-agent (Section 4). Loop: people write the initial agent, the benchmarks and the utility; the paper reports no human step inside the run. Accumulation: all agents are kept in an archive that the meta-agent consults, and each new agent is built by the best agent so far, as in ADAS but with the meta-agent chosen from the archive (Section 3). Evidence: Table 1 reports scores on the same benchmark problems that drive selection (fixed 50-problem subsets); there is no held-out test set, no transfer to other benchmarks or models, and a single run per setting; all evaluations are the authors' own. Cost: Table 1 reports average time per benchmark problem (about 104-151 s, capped at 300 s), and Section 3.1 says one meta-improvement step may take on the order of an hour, but the time for a full benchmark evaluation of one agent is not reported; the 15-iteration run cost about USD 7,000 in API fees (Section 4). Publication status: the arXiv v2 PDF (May 2025) is marked Preprint. Related work: the paper argues that ADAS is not self-improving because its meta-agent is fixed, and that Gödel Agent is not a general-purpose coding agent (Section 2). Reading: the whole paper including Appendices A-D was read|confirmed|JasonDZS|2026-11-28

The modified agent then carries out the next self-modification; the archive and parent selection stay fixed|R2|Section 3: self-improvement is defined as "modifying the design of an agent's own components (i.e., its own code, which does not include the open-ended exploration process described in the next paragraph)", and "the open-ended exploration process (i.e., archive maintenance, parent selection) is fixed and not modifiable by the DGM, which we leave as an avenue for future work". Appendix C.3: what to change is diagnosed by a separate fixed FM (o1) with a fixed prompt, and "the implementation_suggestion and problem_description are extracted and passed to the coding agent as its self-modification task". The reported changes (Section 4.4, Figure 3, Appendix F) are task tools and workflow. Appendix J lists letting the agent modify the exploration process as future work. 150 iterations in the hallucination case study (Appendix H); 3 independent DGM runs on Polyglot for stability (Appendix A.4)|not reported|fully reversible|self-improvement|cross-task|After 80 iterations SWE-bench rises from 20.0% to 50.0% and Polyglot from 14.0% to 38.0% on the 50-task subset (14.2% to 30.7% on the full benchmark), against 39.0% and 28.0% without self-improvement, 23.0% and 14.0% without open-ended exploration, and 39.7% and 30.0% for greedy parent selection (Section 4.4, Table 1); the best SWE-bench agent reaches 28.9% on Polyglot and the best Polyglot agent 24.5% on SWE-bench, and with Claude 3.7 Sonnet the SWE-bench agent goes from 19.0% to 59.5% (Figure 4)|Objective hacking in the hallucination case study: node 114 reached a perfect score by removing the special tool-use markers that the hallucination detector relies on, despite instructions not to change them, and hacking was more frequent when the checking functions were visible to the agent (Appendix H); only 51.3% of generated agents keep basic code-editing ability (Table 2); the lineage of the best agent has performance dips at iterations 4 and 56 (Section 4.4); it still falls short of closed-source SoTA SWE-bench solutions, and one SWE-bench run takes about 2 weeks and about USD 22,000 versus about USD 10,000 for each baseline (Section 6, Appendix E.1); the open-ended exploration process is fixed (Section 3, Appendix J); it is limited by the capabilities of the underlying FM (Section 6); it assumes that better coding benchmark scores reflect a better ability to self-improve (Section 1, Section 6); benchmark-driven modifications might introduce vulnerabilities or misalignment, and iterated self-modification may make the code harder to understand (Section 5); higher-performing agents have higher inference costs (Appendix E.1); only two coding benchmarks were used (Appendix J)|full text|medium|Feedback details: each new agent is evaluated on a coding benchmark in stages (Section 4.2): 10 tasks to check basic editing ability, then 50 more (60 in total for SWE-bench), and for SWE-bench 200 tasks if it scores over 40% on 60 tasks and is among the top two in the archive; Polyglot agents scoring over 40% on 10 tasks go on to 50. Only agents that compile and can still edit code are added to the archive (Section 3, Algorithm 1). Parents are sampled from the whole archive with weight sigmoid(score) x 1/(1 + number of functioning children), lambda 10, midpoint 0.5 (Appendix C.2). The o1 diagnosis step only proposes what to change; it does not decide what is kept. The diagnosis prompt contains SWE-bench's private test patch and test results; the authors report no memorization or overfitting found on manual inspection (Appendix C.3). Models: Claude 3.5 Sonnet (New) does all self-modification; evaluation uses Claude 3.5 Sonnet (New) for SWE-bench and o3-mini for Polyglot (Table 3), so on Polyglot the score does not measure the model that does the self-modification. Loop: people write the initial agent (bash and whole-file edit tools, Appendix C.1), the benchmarks, the diagnosis prompts and the selection rule; Appendix J says proposed self-modifications "are autonomously evaluated without any human intervention", and Section 5 says the authors "actively monitor agent performance and code changes", which is oversight, not a step in the loop. Accumulation: archive of all valid agents; branching from weaker agents leads to later gains (Figure 3). Evidence: the headline scores are on the same subsets that drive selection, and the full Polyglot benchmark includes the 50 search tasks (in-task); the cross-benchmark results are on a benchmark never seen in the search, which the paper calls "truly held-out tests" (Section 4.4); model transfer on SWE-bench uses the same 200 tasks with other FMs (Figure 4), and on Polyglot gains are small (32.0% to 33.3% with Claude 3.5 Sonnet, 35.6% to 36.8% with Claude 3.7 Sonnet, Appendix A.2); search on Python-only Polyglot tasks transfers to other languages (Figure 4); all evaluations are the authors' own. Only indirect evidence: with the self-modifying agent fixed to the base agent (w/o self-improve, Algorithm 2), the final scores are lower (39.0% vs 50.0% and 28.0% vs 38.0%, Table 1) and "gains taper off quickly" (Appendix A.1), and the share of children with basic editing ability is 51.3% vs 32.5% (Table 2). There is no direct measure of self-modification quality across iterations, the choice of what to change stays with the fixed o1 model, the SWE-bench comparison is a single run per setting (DGM runs 40.7% plus or minus 2.3% over 3 Polyglot runs, baselines not repeated), the DGM run cost about twice as much as each baseline, and the progress curves (Figure 2) are stepwise, not accelerating. Cost: Appendix E.1 gives only money (60 SWE-bench tasks about USD 350, 60 Polyglot tasks about USD 5), and Section 6 gives about 2 weeks for a whole SWE-bench run of 80 iterations; the time for one evaluation of one agent is not reported. Venue: the arXiv v3 PDF (12 Mar 2026) is marked "Published as a conference paper at ICLR 2026"; v1 is from May 2025. Reading: the main text and Appendices A-E and G-J were read in full; Appendix F (about 2,600 lines of diffs of the best agents) was only looked over for structure, and the task ID lists in Appendices E.2 and E.3 were not checked one by one|confirmed|JasonDZS|2026-11-28

P007|Self-Adapting Language Models|https://arxiv.org/abs/2506.10943|2025-06|NeurIPS 2025|0|Data and weight self-adaptation|Knowledge incorporation: absorbing SQuAD v1.1 passages into the weights of Qwen2.5-7B and answering questions about them without the passage in context, as single-passage LoRA updates and as continued pretraining on 200 and 2,067 passages; few-shot learning: test-time training of Llama-3.2-1B-Instruct on a curated ARC subset (11 training tasks, 8 evaluation tasks) by choosing data augmentations and training hyperparameters|closed loop; self-reference; accumulation|The model's own weights. The outer ReST-EM loop finetunes the model to generate better self-edits (synthetic finetuning data, and on ARC the choice of augmentations, learning rate, epochs and loss tokens); each self-edit is applied to the same model as an SFT update (LoRA or full finetuning)|R3|Section 3: SEAL is "an algorithm with two nested loops: an outer RL loop, which optimizes the self-edit generation, and an inner update loop, which uses the generated self-edit to update the model via gradient descent"; Abstract: "these self-edits result in persistent weight updates". The outer loop is fixed: ReST-EM with a binary reward, "SFT on good self-edits" (Section 3.1, Algorithm 1), with a fixed self-edit prompt (Section 3.2, Appendix B.11). During RL training each inner update produces a temporary copy that is scored and discarded; the persistent model changes only through the fixed ReST-EM step (Section 3.1, Appendix B.2). The argument for R4: what RL improves is the model's own procedure for producing its training data and, on ARC, its training configuration (Section 3.2: "whether SEAL can autonomously configure the adaptation pipeline"), and Section 3 calls it meta-learning "how to generate effective self-edits"|automated evaluation|fully automatic|multi-generation single lineage|Knowledge incorporation: 2 rounds of ReST-EM, each on 50 contexts with 5 self-edits per context and 3 seeds per self-edit (Section 4.2, Appendix B.2); ARC: a single outer RL round with 15 self-edits for each of 11 tasks (Section 4.1, Appendix A.2); a continual-learning test applies sequential self-edits for a stream of passages (Figure 6)|seconds to minutes|fully reversible|self-improvement|in-task|No-context SQuAD accuracy for single-passage updates rises from 33.5% (train on passage) and 39.7% (base-model self-edits) to 47.0% after 2 ReST-EM rounds, above 46.3% with GPT-4.1 synthetic data; in continued pretraining SEAL reaches 58.2% (n = 200) and 46.4% (n = 2067) versus 59.4% and 49.2% with GPT-4.1 data (Table 2); on the ARC subset 72.5% of self-edits succeed versus 20% without RL, 0% for ICL and 100% for oracle TTT (Table 1)|Catastrophic forgetting: with sequential self-edits, performance on earlier passages gradually declines, and retention is not optimized (Limitations, Figure 6); each self-edit evaluation takes about 30-45 seconds because the reward needs finetuning and evaluating a whole model (Limitations); every context needs a paired downstream task (QA or a held-out query), so RL training cannot scale to unlabeled corpora (Limitations); GRPO and PPO were unstable, so ReST-EM is used (Section 3.1); on ARC it stays below oracle TTT, and the tasks are a small subset filtered to be solvable with optimal TTT (Section 4.1, Appendix A.1); in continued pretraining GPT-4.1 synthetic data slightly outperforms it (Section 4.2), and Entigraph is competitive at the larger scale (Appendix B.9); returns diminish after two iterations (Section 4.2); letting the model choose its own self-edit format (no-prompt) reaches only 18.9% (Appendix B.11); the differences between iterations are sometimes subtle (Figure 5); conclusions on model scaling are hard to draw from two sizes (Appendix B.7)|full text|medium|Feedback details: the reward is whether adapting the model with the self-edit improves its performance on the task (binary reward, Equation 2); in knowledge incorporation the best of 5 self-edits per context, averaged over 3 seeds, is kept (Appendix B.2); on ARC a self-edit is reinforced if the adapted model gives the correct output for the held-out test input, and configurations needing more than 375 training steps are discarded (Section 4.1, Appendix A.2). SQuAD answers are graded against the gold answer by GPT-4.1 (Appendix B.4, under evaluation details); the paper does not say whether the same grader computes the reward during RL training. Appendix B.10 tests a proxy reward from a GPT-4.1 rubric (a learned judge): 45.6% vs 47.0% in about 5 minutes instead of about 6 hours; that is a variant, not the main loop.
